items.title: Kubeflow Pipelines: Pipeline archive upload allows decompression bomb to exhaust server memory
items.description:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server decompresses uploaded pipeline archives without adequately bounding expanded data in affected versions. A small ZIP or gzip-compressed tar archive can consume disproportionately large amounts of memory while the server locates or reads the pipeline file, potentially exhausting API-server resources and interrupting service.

Multipart pipeline and pipeline-version upload processing decompresses the archive before namespace authorization, so a caller who can reach those endpoints does not need a successful pipeline-create authorization decision to trigger the issue. External authentication and network controls can restrict reachability. URL-import handlers authorize before fetching and decompressing a remote archive.

items.title: Kubeflow Pipelines: Run-log endpoint permits unauthorized access to pod logs
items.description:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server's `GET /apis/v1alpha1/runs/{run_id}/nodes/{node_id}/log` handler retrieves logs without authorizing the caller against the selected run. A caller who can reach the backend and knows a victim run ID and a suitable pod or node identifier can read live or archived logs using the API server's permissions.

For live logs, the vulnerable handler also accepts the supplied node ID as a pod name in the run's namespace without verifying that the pod belongs to the run. Depending on the API server's pod-log permissions, a known run ID can therefore permit reading the `main` container logs of an unrelated pod in that namespace. Logs may contain sensitive workload data or credentials.

@hapi/content: quadratic-time parsing of Content-Disposition parameters allows denial of service
items.description:
### Summary

`Content.disposition()` takes quadratic time when a `Content-Disposition` parameter contains a long token without `=`. One unauthenticated multipart request can block the Node.js event loop for several minutes.

### Details

`Content.disposition()` reads the parameters with a global regular expression in `String.prototype.replace()`:

```js
/([^\=\*\s]+)(\*)?\s*\=\s*(?:([^;'"\s]+\'[\w-]*\'[^;\s]+)|(?:\"([^"]*)\")|([^;\s]*))/g
```

The parameter name part `([^\=\*\s]+)` has no anchor. When a run of name characters has no `=` after it, the match attempt reads the full run and fails. The global scan then starts again at the next character and reads the remaining run again. The total time is proportional to the square of the run length.

items.title: Glob: AbortSignal cancellation bypass allows post-timeout filesystem traversal
items.description:
### Summary

In glob 13.0.6, an aborted async walk rejects or emits an error but continues recursively reading directories in the background.

The root cause is that abort branches in src/walker.ts call cb() without returning. As a result, callers that rely on signal or AbortSignal.timeout() to bound glob traversal cost can still incur filesystem I/O and CPU work after the request has already been rejected.

### Details

This was reproduced on glob v13.0.6 (commit e80cb38ae60d6cbff9e75f39032a994858994d35).

- GlobUtil.walkCB()
- GlobUtil.walkCB2()
- GlobUtil.walkCBSync()
- GlobUtil.walkCB2Sync()

items.title: Authlib RFC 7592 examples omit registration-access-token client binding
items.description:
## Description

### Summary

RFC 7592 (OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Management Protocol) lets a previously registered client read, update, or delete its own registration, authenticated by a `registration_access_token` issued specifically to that client at registration time. items.title: pyasn1 has quadratic CPU consumption in constructed BIT STRING decoding
items.description:
## Summary

In pyasn1 through 0.6.4, decoding a constructed BIT STRING with many fragments repeatedly shifts and copies the entire value accumulated so far. For fixed-size fragments, CPU time grows quadratically with the encoded input size. An application that passes sufficiently large, attacker-controlled ASN.1 data to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion during `decode()`; no conversion or formatting of the decoded value is required.

The BER and CER decoders reach this path for constructed BIT STRING values, with or without an `asn1Spec`. The DER decoder rejects constructed BIT STRING in schema-less decoding, but its schema-driven path accepts a **definite-length** constructed BIT STRING when given a matching `asn1Spec` and reaches the same vulnerable code. items.title: pyasn1 has quadratic-complexity denial of service in binary REAL decoding
items.description:
## Summary

In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a binary-encoded ASN.1 REAL with a large mantissa can consume CPU time quadratic in the mantissa length. The BER, CER, and DER decoders all use the affected `RealPayloadDecoder`. An application is exposed when it passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 containing a REAL value to one of these decoders, either without an `asn1Spec` or with a schema that includes REAL. The work occurs inside `decode()`; the application does not need to convert, print, or otherwise use the resulting REAL object.

This is distinct from [CVE-2026-59886](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hm4w-wwcw-mr6r), which concerns converting an already-decoded REAL to a Python float. That issue was fixed in 0.6.4 and its advisory states that decoding alone does not trigger it.

items.title: pyasn1 has quadratic-time denial of service in constructed string and indefinite-length ANY decoding
items.description:
## Summary

In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a constructed OCTET STRING or character string made of many fragments can spend disproportionate CPU time repeatedly copying the accumulated value. A separate indefinite-length `ANY` path has the same problem while collecting the encoded components. The work grows roughly quadratically with the number of fixed-size fragments, although the input and decoded value grow linearly. An application that lets an attacker supply such ASN.1 input to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion.

The affected string paths are available in BER and CER. The DER decoder also accepts certain *non-DER* constructed strings: a definite-length constructed OCTET STRING when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.OctetString`, and constructed character strings such as UTF8String even without a schema. items.title: pyasn1 has quadratic CPU use in schemaless BER/CER/DER container decoding
items.description:
### Summary

When an application decodes attacker-controlled BER, CER, or DER data without an ASN.1 schema, a container with many distinct long tag IDs can cause quadratic CPU use. Repeated inputs can exhaust CPU and reduce service availability.

### Details

ConstructedPayloadDecoderBase._decodeComponentsSchemaless inserts every decoded component’s TagSet into a growing set, although it only needs to distinguish one tag set from two or more. Attacker-chosen tag IDs can have colliding TagSet hashes, making each later insertion compare against an increasing number of earlier tags. This path is present in v0.6.4 and is inherited by the CER and DER decoders. The proposed fix stops growing the classification set after it contains two distinct tag sets, while retaining every decoded component and its order. items.title: Forge: ASN.1 OID first arc truncation in asn1.oidToDer
items.description:
### Summary

`asn1.oidToDer()` did not range-check the first two arcs of an OID string, so an OID such as `0.42.840.113549.1.1.1` or `4294977127.18.840.113549.1.1.1` was encoded as the DER of a different OID (here rsaEncryption, `1.2.840.113549.1.1.1`). This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-66030. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

X.690 section 8.19 encodes the first two arcs of an OID as one subidentifier, `40 * arc1 + arc2`, where the first arc is 0, 1 or 2 and the second arc is at most 39 when the first is 0 or 1. `asn1.oidToDer()` in `lib/asn1.js` computed that value with no range check and wrote it with `putByte()`, which keeps only the low 16 bits. Out-of-range first arcs therefore produced the encoding of a different OID: `0.42.840.113549.1.1.1` gives `40 * 0 + 42 = 42` and `4294977127.18.840.113549.1.1.1` wraps to 42, both the first byte of rsaEncryption. items.description:
### Summary
The `forge.http` client stored cookies from `Set-Cookie` response headers in a plain object keyed by cookie name and path. A malicious server could use the cookie name `__proto__` to add properties to `Object.prototype`, use inherited names such as `constructor` to add properties to `Object`, and send an empty cookie value to delete `Object.prototype` properties. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

`client.setCookie()` in `lib/http.js` stored a cookie with `client.cookies[cookie.name][cookie.path] = cookie`, creating `client.cookies[cookie.name]` only when `!(cookie.name in client.cookies)`. Both values come from the server's `Set-Cookie` header via `response.getCookies()`. Because `in` also sees inherited properties:

items.description:
### Summary
The forge TLS client's check for a missing server certificate read the wrong property and never ran. A malicious TLS server, or an on-path attacker who removes the server's Certificate message, can make `connection.process()` throw a `TypeError`, which crashes applications that use the forge TLS client. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

The check tested `c.serverCertificate`, which is never set (the certificate is stored as `c.session.serverCertificate`), so it never ran. items.title: Forge: Regular expression denial of service in PEM decoding (pem.decode)
items.description:
### Summary
`pem.decode()`, which every node-forge API that parses PEM input uses, split messages with a regular expression that takes polynomial time on input without a matching END line, and parsed encapsulated headers with regular expressions that take quadratic time on long header lines. A remote attacker can block the Node.js event loop for seconds to minutes with a crafted input of a few tens of kilobytes. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
`pem.decode()` in `lib/pem.js` found PEM messages with this regular expression:

    /\s*-----BEGIN ([A-Z0-9- ]+)-----\r?\n?([\x21-\x7e\s]+?(?:\r?\n\r?\n))?([:A-Za-z0-9+\/=\s]+?)-----END \1-----/g

items.title: Forge: Denial of Service via infinite loop in BigInteger.modInverse() with negative input (incomplete fix of CVE-2026-33891)
items.description:
### Summary

`BigInteger.prototype.modInverse()` in node-forge's bundled jsbn library enters an infinite loop when the value or the modulus is negative, for example when a negative public exponent is passed to `forge.pki.rsa.generateKeyPair()`. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2026-33891 (GHSA-5m6q-g25r-mvwx), which handled only a zero value. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

`bnModInverse()` (`lib/jsbn.js`, exposed as `forge.jsbn.BigInteger.prototype.modInverse`) implements the binary extended Euclidean algorithm (Handbook of Applied Cryptography, Algorithm 14.61), which is defined for positive integers. With a negative operand the loop cannot terminate: `rShiftTo` is an arithmetic shift, so a negative value never moves towards zero, and the loop's exit condition (`u` reaching zero) is never met. items.title: Forge: verifyCertificateChain() removes trusted CA certificates with the same subject from the CA store
items.description:
### Summary

When a CA store created by `pki.createCaStore()` holds two or more certificates with the same subject name, `pki.verifyCertificateChain()` permanently removes those certificates from the store while trying each one as the issuer. A peer can send any certificate that names that subject as its issuer to make all later verifications against those CA certificates fail. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

`pki.verifyCertificateChain()` (`lib/x509.js`) asks the CA store for the issuer of each certificate with `caStore.getIssuer()`. When the store holds several certificates with the same subject, `caStore.getIssuer()` returns the store's own internal array of those certificates (`caStore.certs[hash]`, built by `addCertificate()`). `verifyCertificateChain()` used that array directly as its list of candidate parents and called `parents.shift()` on it while trying each candidate.

items.title: Forge: AES-GCM authentication bypass via unvalidated tagLength option
items.description:
### Summary

The AES-GCM mode in forge.cipher does not validate the tagLength option passed to start(). With a tagLength of 0 or a value that converts to 0 (such as null, false, '' or '0'), the authentication tag is empty, and decipher.finish() returns true for any ciphertext and additional data when the supplied tag is empty or missing. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

`modes.gcm.prototype.start()` in `lib/cipherModes.js` stored the `tagLength` option without validation, and `lib/cipher.js` documented it as accepting "0-128". After processing the data, `afterFinish()` truncates the 16-byte tag with `truncate(16 % (tagLength / 8))`. For a `tagLength` that converts to 0, this is `16 % 0 = NaN`, and truncating by `NaN` empties the tag. items.title: Forge: PKCS#12 MAC forgery and constant-key PBE via zero iteration count
items.description:
### Summary

forge.pkcs12.pkcs12FromAsn1() accepts a PKCS#12 MAC iteration count of zero (or less) from the input, and the PKCS#12 key derivation function then returns a constant key that does not depend on the password or salt. An attacker who does not know the password can modify a PKCS#12/PFX file and compute a MAC that verifies with any password; PKCS#12 PBE-encrypted private keys prepared the same way decrypt with any password. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

`p12.pkcs12FromAsn1()` in `lib/pkcs12.js` reads the MAC iteration count (`MacData.iterations`) from the input and passes it to the PKCS#12 key derivation function `pki.pbe.generatePkcs12Key()` in `lib/pbe.js` (also exposed as `forge.pkcs12.generateKey()`) without checking that it is at least 1. items.description:
### Summary

A connection created with `forge.tls.createConnection()` throws an uncaught `TypeError` from `process()` when it receives a record of another content type while waiting for the rest of a handshake message that was split across records. items.description:
### Summary

Connections created with `forge.tls.createConnection()` processed received TLS records recursively, one stack level per record. A peer can send one chunk of thousands of small records, such as heartbeat records, which are accepted before the handshake, and `process()` throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`, which terminates Node.js processes that use the documented socket wiring. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

In `lib/tls.js`, `c.process()` reads one record and passes it to `_update()`, which calls the handler for the record type from `ctTable`. Every handler (`tls.handleHeartbeat`, `tls.handleApplicationData`, `tls.handleHandshake` for fragmented messages, `tls.handleHelloRequest` and the other handshake handlers) ends by calling `c.process()` again to continue with the next buffered record, or the next message in the same record. items.title: Forge: X.509 basicConstraints bypass in verifyCertificateChain() via deprecated extension OIDs 2.5.29.10 and 2.5.29.13
items.description:
### Summary
node-forge parses certificate extensions with the deprecated OIDs `2.5.29.10` and `2.5.29.13` as `basicConstraints`, and `forge.pki.verifyCertificateChain()` used the first extension with that name. A certificate with a forged deprecated-OID extension (`cA` TRUE) before its genuine `basicConstraints` extension (`cA` FALSE) is accepted as a CA certificate, and the same technique can hide a `pathLenConstraint`. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

`lib/oids.js` maps the deprecated certificate extension OIDs `2.5.29.10` and `2.5.29.13` to the name `basicConstraints`, the same name as the RFC 5280 extension `2.5.29.19`. `certificateExtensionFromAsn1()` in `lib/x509.js` decodes extensions by name, so these extensions are decoded into the same `cA` and `pathLenConstraint` fields. `cert.getExtension()` returns the first extension with a matching name, and `pki.verifyCertificateCh

items.title: PHPUnit vulnerable to code execution by other local users via shared temporary directory in PHPT code coverage handling
items.description:
### Summary

When PHPT tests are run with code coverage, PHPUnit 13.4.0 to 13.4.3 writes the code of each PHPT test to a directory with a fixed name below the operating system's path used for temporary files, for instance `/tmp/phpunit-phpt` on Linux, and executes it from there. PHPUnit uses this directory even when it was created by another user.

On a system where the path used for temporary files is shared between users, another local user can create this directory before the developer runs PHPUnit, replace the code of a PHPT test before it is executed, and thereby execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the developer. The test still passes and the code coverage report is complete, so the attack is not visible.

The impact is full code execution as the user who runs PHPUnit. The likelihood is low: the attacker needs an account on the same system and must create the directory bef

items.title: Nuxt dev server exposes generated appSecret through Vite file serving
items.description:
### Impact

When no `appSecret` is configured (via `NUXT_APP_SECRET`, `NITRO_APP_SECRET` or `runtimeConfig.appSecret`), `nuxt dev` generates a development secret and stores it in `<buildDir>/app-secret` (by default `.nuxt/app-secret`). The build directory is inside the directories that Nuxt passes to Vite's `server.fs.allow`, so the file can be fetched from the dev server:

```bash
curl http://<dev-server>/_nuxt/@fs/<absolute-path-to-project>/.nuxt/app-secret
```

Anyone who can read it can compute every secret derived from it with `deriveSecret()`, including the default password used by `useSession`, and so can forge session cookies accepted by that dev server.

Nuxt dev server arbitrary file read through client error reports
items.description:
### Summary

A client that can connect to the dev server's HMR socket can send a `nuxt:dev:client-error` event whose message ends in an absolute file path. The dev server reads that file while building the error report, and its contents are returned in the error overlay, on the dev error channel, and in the report shown in the terminal.

### Impact

This affects the development server only; production builds contain none of this code. Affected versions are `4.6.0` to `4.6.2`.

Reading the file requires TCP access to the dev server, so the default localhost bind limits this to local processes, which can usually read the same files directly. items.title: Nuxt dev server exposes private runtime config through the Nitro dev bundle
items.description:
### Summary

With Nitro 2 (the default server engine in Nuxt 3 and Nuxt 4), the Nitro development server bundle written by `nuxt dev` can be fetched through the Vite dev server. Nitro inlines the resolved `runtimeConfig` into that bundle, so private runtime config values that were resolved at build time can be read by anyone with HTTP access to the dev server.

### Impact

`nuxt dev` writes the Nitro development server bundle to `<buildDir>/dev/index.mjs` (by default `.nuxt/dev/index.mjs`). The build directory is inside the directories Nuxt passes to Vite's `server.fs.allow`, so the bundle is served by the dev server:

```bash
curl http://<dev-server>/_nuxt/@fs/<absolute-path-to-project>/.nuxt/dev/index.mjs
```

items.description:
## Summary

MariaDB Connector/J sized heap allocations from lengths declared by the server
in OK packets before checking that those lengths fit in the packet. A rogue or
MitM server can make the client allocate megabytes from a packet of a few bytes.

## Details

When `CLIENT_SESSION_TRACK` is negotiated (the default), an OK packet carries an

server-declared `len`, then copied the packet data into it. The copy failed with an
`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` when the packet was shorter, but only after the
allocation had taken place.

items.title: MariaDB Connector/J: Length-encoded integers larger than Integer.MAX_VALUE were truncated before being used as lengths
items.description:
## Summary

MariaDB Connector/J narrowed 8-byte length-encoded integers received from the
server to `int` without validation. A rogue or MitM server can send a value above
`Integer.MAX_VALUE` whose truncation becomes a negative or arbitrary length.

## Details

The protocol encodes lengths as length-encoded integers, whose 8-byte form the
decoder (`readLength()` and `readIntLengthEncodedNotNull()`) returned as
`(int) readLong()`. A value above `Integer.MAX_VALUE` therefore wrapped to a
negative or unrelated `int`, used afterwards as a length to size allocations or
reads, which ended in `NegativeArraySizeException`, out-of-bounds exceptions or
oversized allocations.

The fix rejects any length-encoded value that does not fit a non-negative `int`
with an explicit error.

client's connection handling w

items.title: MariaDB Connector/J: XA recover() trusted server-supplied gtrid and bqual lengths
items.description:
## Summary

`XAResource.recover()` in MariaDB Connector/J trusted the `gtrid_length` and
`bqual_length` columns returned by `XA RECOVER` to allocate and split each Xid.

## Details

`MariaDbPoolConnection` and `MariaDbPoolPinnedConnection` built each `Xid` of
the recovery list by allocating `new byte[gtrid_length]` and
`new byte[bqual_length]` and copying from the `data` column, without validating
the lengths against the XA specification bounds (`Xid.MAXGTRIDSIZE`,
`Xid.MAXBQUALSIZE`) or the actual payload. Negative or oversized lengths, or
lengths that do not fit the data, ended in large allocations or unchecked
exceptions (`NegativeArraySizeException`, `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`)
during recovery.

The fix validates the lengths before any allocation or copy and reports an
invalid row as an `XAException` (`XAER_RMFAIL`).
